docs.title: What is bobbie?
docs.text: Named after Roberta Draper ("Bobbie") from "The Expanse," bobbie provides a lightweight and easy-to-use way to store and access configuration settings for a Python project.

docs.title: Why use bobbie?
docs.text:
There are numerous options for storing configuration settings in Python. So, what makes bobbie different?

  • Flexible: a Settings instance is easily built from a dict, Python module, or file (ini, json, toml, and yaml formats are supported).
  • Lightweight: an efficient codebase ensures a very small memory footprint.
  • Intuitive: a create class method constructs Settings (from any data source).
  • Portable: Settings can be exported to any of the supported file types, so settings built in code can be saved as a settings file.
  • Convenient: unlike configparser, values stored as strings (such as in ini files) are automatically converted to the matching Python types when Settings is created.

The comparison table below shows how bobbie compares to the other major options that store configuration options for Python projects.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
To install bobbie, use pip:

pip install bobbie

Loading and exporting yaml files requires the yaml extra, which adds PyYAML. Exporting toml files requires the toml extra, which adds tomli-w:

pip install "bobbie[toml,yaml]"

docs.title: Create a Settings instance
docs.text: bobbie supports several ways to create a Settings instance. You can either: * If the settings are in a file, call a class method specific to the file type (from_yaml in the second example below); * Call a class method for the general type of source data (from_dict or from_file); * Call the create class method and it will automatically figure out the appropriate constructor; or * If the settings data is in a dict-like object, pass it as the first argument to Settings.

docs.title: From a dict
docs.text:
import bobbie

configuration = {
  'general': {
    'verbose': False,
    'seed': 43,
    'parallelize': False},
  'files': {
    'source_format': 'csv',
    'file_encoding': 'windows-1252',
    'float_format': '%.4f',
    'export_results': True}}
# You can pick a specific constructor method.
settings = bobbie.Settings.from_dict(configuration)
# Or, may use the general `create` method.
settings = bobbie.Settings.create(configuration)
# Or, just send a `dict` to `Settings` itself.
settings = bobbie.Settings(configuration)

docs.title: From a file
docs.text:
import bobbie

# You may use the general `create` method.
settings = bobbie.Settings.create('settings_file.yaml')
# Or, the `from_file` method.
settings = bobbie.Settings.from_file('settings_file.yaml')
# Or, the `from_yaml` method. They all do the same thing.
settings = bobbie.Settings.from_yaml('settings_file.yaml')

If the file is a Python module, it must contain a variable named settings in the module namespace (unless you change the global setting for the variable name).

docs.title: Type inference
docs.text:
ini and json files often store numbers, booleans, and lists as strings, so bobbie converts their values to the matching Python types:

  • '42' becomes 42 and '2.5' becomes 2.5.
  • 'true', 'yes', 'false', and 'no' (in any case) become True or False.
  • '[x, y, z]' and 'x, y, z' become ['x', 'y', 'z']. A comma followed by a line break also splits a list, so a list can span several lines of an ini file, but a comma with nothing after it, as in 'x,y', does not split a string.
  • '{a: 1, b: [x, y]}' becomes {'a': 1, 'b': ['x', 'y']}.

Items in lists and dicts are converted the same way and may be nested. Put an item in quotes (such as ["a, b", '1']) to keep it as a string.

toml, yaml, and Python module values are not converted because those formats already store their own types. So, a toml value of "[a, b]" stays a string. See the Advanced User Guide for the exact rules and how to turn inference on or off for each file type.

docs.title: Export settings to a file
docs.text:
bobbie can also create a settings file from a Settings instance. You can either: * Call the method specific to the file type (to_ini, to_json, to_module, to_toml, or to_yaml); or * Call the to_file method and it will pick the appropriate method from the file extension.

import bobbie

settings = bobbie.Settings.create('settings_file.yaml')
settings.add('general', {'seed': 7})
# You may use the general `to_file` method.
settings.to_file('settings_file.toml')
# Or, the `to_toml` method. They both do the same thing.
settings.to_toml('settings_file.toml')

Any additional keyword arguments are passed to the writer for the file type (such as indent for json.dump). An existing file is overwritten.

Exported files can be loaded back into the same Settings. For ini files, lists and dicts are written in the form that type inference reads (such as [x, y, z]), and items that would otherwise be converted are quoted. Because ini files store everything as strings, every top-level value must be a section (a dict), and a string that looks like another type (such as '42') is loaded as that type. A Settings exported with to_module stores its values in a module-level variable named settings. See the Advanced User Guide for the arguments each exporter accepts and the other ini limits.

docs.title: Similar projects
docs.text: There are a lot of great packages for storing project settings. The table below shows the features of the leading libraries.

docs.title: Feature Comparison of Python Configuration Libraries
docs.text:
Library Typing Secrets Export dict ini json py toml yaml bobbie ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ configparser ✅ ✅ dynaconf ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ Parser-it ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ python-decouple ✅ ✅ ✅ pyconfig ✅ pydantic-settings ✅ ✅

As you can see, bobbie lacks a method for storing passwords, encryption keys, and other secrets. That is because it is focused on internal Python projects and the goal of keeping its resource usage as low as possible. So, if you need secrets stored in your project settings, there are several good options linked above that you should explore.

docs.title: Advanced User Guide
docs.text: This guide covers the parts of bobbie beyond the Tutorial: how create chooses a constructor, passing arguments to the file parsers, the exact type inference rules, the global options, and extending Settings.

docs.title: How create works
docs.text:
Settings.create dispatches on the type of its first argument:

Source type Constructor str or pathlib.Path from_file MutableMapping (such as a dict) from_dict Anything else raises TypeError

from_file then looks up the file extension in bobbie.options._FILE_EXTENSIONS and calls the matching from_<type> class method (from_ini, from_json, from_module, from_toml, or from_yaml).

Any keyword arguments that you pass to create or from_file are relayed to that loader, which passes them to its parser.

docs.title: Setting attributes of the new instance
docs.text:
create, from_dict, and from_file accept a parameters dict of arguments for the new Settings itself (such as name or default_factory). They are kept apart from the keyword arguments for the parser:

import decimal

settings = bobbie.Settings.create(
    'settings.toml',
    parameters = {'name': 'Project Settings'},
    parse_float = decimal.Decimal)
settings.name  # 'Project Settings'

An argument in parameters that Settings does not accept raises a TypeError.

docs.title: Parser arguments
docs.text:
Each loader passes its keyword arguments to a different parser:

Loader Keyword arguments go to Useful arguments from_ini configparser.ConfigParser interpolation, delimiters, default_section from_json json.load parse_float, parse_int, object_hook from_module importlib.util.spec_from_file_location rarely needed from_toml tomllib.load parse_float from_yaml ignored (accepted so that create works the same way for every type)

For example, to load toml floats as decimal.Decimal:

import decimal

settings = bobbie.Settings.create('settings.toml', parse_float = decimal.Decimal)

docs.title: File encoding
docs.text:
ini, json, and yaml files are read as UTF-8. Pass encoding to read a file with another encoding:

settings = bobbie.Settings.create('legacy.ini', encoding = 'cp1252')

toml files are always UTF-8, as the toml format requires.

The exporters take encoding too (see Writer arguments).

docs.title: ini files
docs.text:
A few details are specific to ini files:

  • Interpolation is off by default, so values such as %.4f load as they are. To use configparser interpolation (such as %(root)s), pass interpolation = configparser.BasicInterpolation() or configparser.ExtendedInterpolation().
  • Option names keep their case. configparser normally lowercases them, but bobbie does not.
  • The DEFAULT section is not a section of its own. Its options are added to every other section, as configparser does.
  • Comments can follow values. A # with whitespace before and after it starts a comment that runs to the end of its line, on the first line of a value or any line after it. A # without whitespace on both sides (as in #1f77b4 or a#b) is part of the value. Set _INLINE_COMMENTS to False to keep comments in values (see Global options).
  • A list can span several lines, since a comma followed by a line break separates its items (see Type inference rules).
[tasks]
label = target  # the column to predict
steps = stop, drop,  # the first two steps
    roll

settings = bobbie.Settings.create('tasks.ini')
settings['tasks']  # {'label': 'target', 'steps': ['stop', 'drop', 'roll']}

[DEFAULT]
root = /data

[paths]
raw = %(root)s/raw

import configparser

settings = bobbie.Settings.create(
    'paths.ini', interpolation = configparser.BasicInterpolation())
settings['paths']  # {'raw': '/data/raw', 'root': '/data'}

docs.title: Python modules
docs.text: from_module runs the module and reads its settings variable. If the variable is missing, it raises an AttributeError. You can change the variable name with _MODULE_SETTINGS_ATTRIBUTE (see Global options).

docs.title: Writer arguments
docs.text:
Each exporter passes its keyword arguments to a different writer, and some change a default so that the file is easier to read:

Exporter Keyword arguments go to Defaults set by bobbie Useful arguments to_ini configparser.ConfigParser interpolation = None delimiters, encoding to_json json.dump indent = 4 ensure_ascii, sort_keys, encoding to_module pprint.pformat sort_dicts = False width, indent to_toml tomli_w.dump indent, multiline_strings to_yaml yaml.safe_dump sort_keys = False allow_unicode, default_flow_style, encoding

to_file passes its keyword arguments to the exporter for the file type. For example, to write a json file with keys in sorted order:

settings.to_file('settings.json', sort_keys = True)

ini, json, and yaml files are written as UTF-8 unless you pass encoding. json and yaml escape characters that are not ASCII unless you pass ensure_ascii = False or allow_unicode = True. toml files and Python modules are always UTF-8.

docs.title: Exporting ini files
docs.text:
to_ini converts each value to a string that from_ini converts back to the same value:

  • Lists (and tuples) are written in square brackets and dicts in curly braces, such as [stop, drop, roll] and {small: 1, big: [2.5, True]}.
  • Items in a list or dict are quoted when they would otherwise be converted or split, such as ['1', 'a, b', ''].
  • Interpolation is off, as it is when loading, so values such as %.4f are written as they are.

A few values cannot be written so that they load back unchanged:

  • Top-level values outside a section. ini files only hold values inside sections, so to_ini raises a TypeError if a top-level value is not a dict.
  • Strings that look like other types. A string value of '42', 'yes', or 'a, b' in a section is written without quotes (ini values have none) and loads as 42, True, or ['a', 'b']. Turn off type inference for ini files if you need these strings (see Global options).
  • Comments. A # with whitespace before and after it (as in a # b) loads as the start of a comment, even inside quotes. Set _INLINE_COMMENTS to False to keep it.
  • None. It is written as None and loads as the string 'None'.

The other file types store their own types, so they do not have these limits (except that toml has no None and json keys must be strings).

docs.title: Type inference rules
docs.text:
When type inference is on for a file type (by default, ini and json), bobbie converts string values with these rules, in order:

  1. A string that int accepts becomes an int (such as '42', ' 42 ', or '1_000'). So, '1' becomes 1, not True, and '02134' becomes 2134.
  2. A string that float accepts becomes a float (such as '2.5', '1e3', 'nan', or 'inf').
  3. 'true' and 'yes' become True, and 'false' and 'no' become False (in any case). Other words, such as 'on', 'none', or 'null', stay strings.
  4. A string in square brackets (such as '[x, y, z]') becomes a list.
  5. A string in curly braces (such as '{a: 1, b: 2}') becomes a dict if every entry has a key and a value separated by :. Otherwise, it stays a string.
  6. A string that contains a comma followed by whitespace, such as a space or a line break (as in 'x, y, z' or 'x,\ny'), becomes a list. A comma with no whitespace after it (such as 'a,b') does not split the string.
  7. Any other string is unchanged. Values that are not strings (such as json numbers) are never changed.

Items in lists and dicts are converted with the same rules and may be nested (such as '[[1, 2], [3]]'). Commas inside brackets or quotes do not split an item, and quotes around an item keep it as a string and are removed:

Stored string Loaded value '[1, 2.5, true]' [1, 2.5, True] '["a, b", c]' ['a, b', 'c'] "['1']" ['1'] '{a: {b: no}}' {'a': {'b': False}} '{url: "http://x.com"}' {'url': 'http://x.com'} '[x, y], z' [['x', 'y'], 'z'] "x not in ['a', 'b']" "x not in ['a', 'b']"

Inference reaches the values at the top level and the values in each section. Values nested more deeply (such as a json object inside a section) are left as they are.

docs.title: Global options
docs.text:
bobbie.options stores the module-level options that Settings uses. They are private (their names start with _), but you can change them to adjust bobbie for a whole project. Change them before loading any settings.

Option Default Effect _INFER_TYPES {'ini': True, 'json': True, 'toml': False, 'module': False, 'yaml': False} Whether to infer types for each file type. _MODULE_SETTINGS_ATTRIBUTE 'settings' Name of the variable that holds the settings in a Python module. _OVERWRITE_ATTRIBUTES True Default for the overwrite argument of inject. _FILE_EXTENSIONS {'ini': 'ini', 'json': 'json', 'toml': 'toml', 'py': 'module', 'yaml': 'yaml', 'yml': 'yaml'} Maps file extensions to file types (and so to from_<type> loaders and to_<type> exporters). _TYPER bobbie.utilities._typify Function used to infer the type of each value. _INLINE_COMMENTS True Whether to remove comments after values in ini files. _ALWAYS_RETURN_ERROR False Default for the return_error argument of delete (and so whether del raises a KeyError for a missing key).

For example:

from bobbie import options

# Keeps `json` values exactly as they are stored.
options._INFER_TYPES['json'] = False
# Reads settings from a `CONFIG` variable in Python modules.
options._MODULE_SETTINGS_ATTRIBUTE = 'CONFIG'

docs.title: Defaults for missing keys
docs.text:
Settings can return a default for missing keys, like collections.defaultdict. The default is only used by get, not by [].

Set it with the default_factory argument or the setdefault method. If the default is callable, get calls it and returns the result. Otherwise, get returns the default itself:

settings = bobbie.Settings({'general': {'seed': 43}}, default_factory = dict)
settings.get('database')  # {}

settings.setdefault('missing')
settings.get('database')  # 'missing'
settings['database']  # KeyError

A default passed to get takes priority over default_factory. Because None means "no default," get cannot return None as a fallback. Set default_factory to lambda: None if you need that.

docs.title: Differences from dict
docs.text:
Settings behaves like a dict in most ways, with these exceptions:

  • get raises a KeyError for a missing key when there is no default (instead of returning None).
  • setdefault(value) sets the default for get (see above). It does not take a key.
  • del settings[key] does nothing if key is missing (unless _ALWAYS_RETURN_ERROR is True).
  • update, +, and += merge the options within each section (see the Tutorial) instead of replacing whole sections.
  • fromkeys returns a Settings and accepts keyword arguments for it (such as name).
  • A Settings is a dataclass, so == compares it to other Settings instances and is False for a plain dict. Compare settings.contents to a dict instead.
  • Sections are not attributes. Use settings['general'], not settings.general.

docs.title: Subclassing and new file types
docs.text:
Settings is a dataclass, so you can subclass it to add fields or methods. The class methods (create, from_file, and the loaders) return an instance of the subclass.

To support another file type, add a from_<type> class method that returns an instance, and map the extension to <type> in options._FILE_EXTENSIONS. Call _infer_types on the loaded contents if the format stores values as strings. For example, for a file of section.option = value lines:

import pathlib
from typing import Any

import bobbie
from bobbie import options


class ProjectSettings(bobbie.Settings):
    """Settings that can also load ".conf" files."""

    @classmethod
    def from_conf(
            cls,
            source: pathlib.Path | str,
            **kwargs: Any) -> ProjectSettings:
        """Creates an instance from a ".conf" file."""
        contents: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}
        text = pathlib.Path(source).read_text(encoding = 'utf-8')
        for line in text.splitlines():
            if '=' in line:
                key, value = line.split('=', 1)
                section, option = key.strip().split('.', 1)
                contents.setdefault(section, {})[option] = value.strip()
        return cls(cls._infer_types(contents))


options._FILE_EXTENSIONS['conf'] = 'conf'
settings = ProjectSettings.create('project.conf')

Only ProjectSettings can load the new file type. Loading a ".conf" file with bobbie.Settings raises a TypeError, because it has no from_conf method.

To export the new file type too, add a to_<type> method that takes the path and keyword arguments. to_file finds it through the same extension mapping:

class ProjectSettings(bobbie.Settings):
    """Settings that can also load and export ".conf" files."""

    # from_conf as above.

    def to_conf(self, path: pathlib.Path | str, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        """Exports the settings to a ".conf" file."""
        lines = [
            f'{section}.{option} = {value}'
            for section, options in self.items()
            for option, value in options.items()]
        pathlib.Path(path).write_text('\n'.join(lines) + '\n', encoding = 'utf-8')


settings.to_file('copy.conf')

Exporting a ".conf" file with bobbie.Settings raises a TypeError, because it has no to_conf method.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

• Added export methods to Settings that create a settings file from its contents: to_ini, to_json, to_module, to_toml, and to_yaml, plus to_file, which picks the method from the file extension (as from_file does). Keyword arguments are passed to the writer for the file type (encoding sets the encoding of ini, json, and yaml files, which defaults to UTF-8, as it does for the loaders), and exported files load back into the same Settings.
  • to_ini writes lists and dicts in the form that type inference reads (such as [x, y, z]) and quotes items that would otherwise be converted. It raises a TypeError if a top-level value is not a section.
  • Added a toml extra that installs tomli-w, which to_toml requires.
  • Added an "Export" column to the feature comparison in the README and documented exporting in the README, Tutorial, Advanced User Guide (writer arguments, ini limits, and exporting new file types), and Recipes.
  • Added tests for exporting every file type (70 tests in total).

• The API documentation now has one page for each public object (the names in __all__), so it only documents Settings, and only once. Before, it had a page for every module, including the private options and utilities, and showed Settings twice.
  • The Settings page now includes the public methods inherited from bunches.Dictionary (fromkeys, setdefault, and subset) and leaves out the unused sources attribute inherited from wonka.Sourcerer.
  • Added a griffe extension so that section markers (such as """ Class Methods """) after an attribute are not shown as that attribute's description.
  • Type inference now splits a list on a comma followed by any whitespace, not only a space, so an ini list can span several lines (steps = a, b, followed by an indented c). Before, a comma at the end of a line did not split the value.
  • Possibly breaking: ini files can have comments after values. A # with whitespace before and after it starts a comment that runs to the end of its line (as in label = target # the column to predict), on any line of a value. A # without whitespace on both sides (as in #1f77b4 or a#b) is kept. Set options._INLINE_COMMENTS to False to keep comments in values, as before.

• Fixed type inference, which raised a RecursionError for strings with a ", " only inside brackets, parentheses, or quotes (such as an ini value of see (a, b)). Those strings now stay strings.
  • Fixed Settings.create and Settings.from_file, which passed parameters to the file parser (raising a TypeError) instead of to the new Settings, as the Settings docstring describes.
  • Possibly breaking: ini, json, and yaml files are now read as UTF-8 instead of the platform's default encoding for json and yaml (such as cp1252 on Windows). Pass encoding to read another encoding.
  • Fixed options._ALWAYS_RETURN_ERROR, which was read once at import, so changing it had no effect on delete and del.
  • A file type in options._FILE_EXTENSIONS with no from_<type> loader now raises the documented TypeError instead of an AttributeError. A Python module without a settings variable now raises an AttributeError that names the variable, instead of a TypeError saying that modules are not supported.
  • Removed the Settings.sources class attribute, which create never used (it dispatches with functools.singledispatchmethod).
  • Added default_factory to the Settings fields so that it appears in the API documentation and mkdocs build --strict passes.
  • Removed the "To Do" sections from the module docstrings so that they do not appear in the documentation.
  • Wrote the Tutorial, Advanced User Guide, and Recipes pages of the documentation, documented the yaml extra in the README, and fixed the README comparison table and links. Added the docs build, lint, and mypy commands to the Contribution Guide.
  • Added tests for the fixes above (51 tests in total).
• Added the py.typed marker so that type checkers use the type hints in bobbie.

• Breaking: settings + other now returns a new Settings and leaves both operands unchanged. Use settings += other to add other in place (the old behavior of "+").
  • Removed the claim that Settings.create accepts a sequence of paths or mappings, which it never supported. Passing one raises a TypeError.
  • Removed the commented-out env and xml loaders and their options.
  • Updated to the snickerdoodle 0.5.0 template (Codecov coverage, a coverage page in the docs, pydoclint, Python 3.15, SPDX license metadata, a version read from __version__, GitHub CLI releases, and uv updates from Dependabot). Added .cruft.json so that cruft update can apply future template changes.
  • Removed the leftovers from pdm (pdm.lock and the credits page and script, which read pdm.lock) and moved the issue templates out of a nested ISSUE_TEMPLATE folder.
  • Now requires bunches 0.3.0 and wonka 0.3.0 or later, which ship type information, so mypy checks Settings against its base classes. The intentional differences from bunches.Dictionary (add, update, items, keys, and values) are marked with # type: ignore[override].
  • Settings now inherits fromkeys, setdefault, and subset from bunches.Dictionary instead of repeating them. subset now deep copies the values chosen with include (before, they were shared with the original) and accepts a returns argument ("class", "copy", or "simple"). fromkeys now accepts any iterable of keys and defaults value to None, as dict.fromkeys does.
  • Documented type inference in the README, including that toml, yaml, and Python module values are not converted, and removed the README acknowledgments.
  • Added conversion of list and dict strings to Python lists and dicts when inferring types (such as from ini files). [x, y, z] becomes ['x', 'y', 'z'] and {a: 1, b: [x, y]} becomes {'a': 1, 'b': ['x', 'y']}. Items are converted recursively, may be nested, and may be quoted to keep commas or prevent conversion.
  • Splitting strings on ", " into lists now ignores commas inside brackets or quotes.
  • Fixed Settings.from_toml, which ignored its keyword arguments (such as parse_float).
  • Fixed Settings.from_yaml, which raised a TypeError when given any keyword arguments. They are now accepted and ignored.
  • Fixed loading a file with an unsupported extension, which raised a KeyError instead of the documented TypeError.
  • Fixed the Settings.create example in the docstring, which was not valid Python.
  • Restyled the package (single quotes, spaces around keyword argument =, closing brackets on the last line, and complete docstrings). Ruff now enforces single quotes and the 80 character line limit.
  • mypy now passes and runs in CI. yaml is treated as an untyped import.
  • Removed the ruff format pre-commit hook, which would undo the package style, and set ruff's force-exclude so pre-commit does not lint excluded folders.
  • Added tests for the dict methods, inject, subset, fromkeys, missing and unsupported files, keyword arguments, and the private utilities (44 tests in total).

• Fixed loading ini files with values that contain a "%" (such as float_format = %.4f), which raised a configparser.InterpolationSyntaxError. Interpolation is now off by default and can be turned back on with interpolation = configparser.BasicInterpolation().
  • Fixed loading a missing ini file, which was silently ignored instead of raising a FileNotFoundError.
  • Fixed Settings.inject, which ignored its overwrite and sections arguments.
  • Fixed Settings.keys, which called itself forever and raised a RecursionError.
• Stable release version with all tests and lint checks passed

• Switched to uv as dependency manager
  • Updated GitHub Actions and dependencies
  • Added full support for yaml and toml
  • Removed support for env (not nested) and xml (rarely used)

• Fixed GitHub actions bug with pdm and ruff
  • Fixed typo in readme

• Added documentation and readme
  • Added more tests
  • Added .env support
  • Changed required Python version to 3.11 or later
• Changelogs not stored before the transitition to the snickerdoodle template

docs.title: Environment Setup
docs.text:
Install uv, then create a virtual environment with all of the development dependencies from the repository folder:

uv sync

Then, install the pre-commit hooks so that they run before each commit:

uv run pre-commit install

Run the tests with uv run pytest.

Before you push, also run the linter and the type checker, which CI runs:

uv run ruff check --no-fix
uv run mypy

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is built with MkDocs. The "Coverage Report" page reads the HTML coverage report in htmlcov, so create it first, and then preview the site:

uv run pytest --cov --cov-report=html
uv run mkdocs serve

The API pages are generated from the docstrings in src/bobbie, so update them when you change a public class or method.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Follow this basic process:

  1. Fork and clone the repository.
  2. Create a new branch: git checkout -b feature-or-bugfix-name.
  3. Edit the code.
  4. If you added functionality or features, update the documentation accordingly.

If you are unsure about how to fix or ignore a warning, just let the continuous integration fail, and we will help you during review.

Don't bother updating the changelog, we will take care of this.

docs.title: Pull requests guidelines
docs.text:
Link to any related issue in the Pull Request message.

During the review, we recommend using fixups:

# SHA is the SHA of the commit you want to fix
git commit --fixup=SHA

Once all the changes are approved, you can squash your commits:

git rebase -i --autosquash main

And force-push:

git push -f

If this seems all too complicated, you can push or force-push each new commit, and we will squash them ourselves if needed, before merging.

docs.title: Style Guidelines
docs.text:
This package follows the Google Python Style Guide with two notable exceptions:

  1. It always adds spaces around "=". This not only violates the Google guide, it violates PEP8, the foundational Python style guide from which all other resources are derived. I defy this strong, long-standing norm because I find it more readable. My brain and eyes have trouble seeing two separate objects when an equal sign is in the middle. I imagine that I am not alone in this accessibility issue. Further, as PEP8 itself notes, required spaces around equal signs are becoming increasing common with type annotations becoming part of best practices (and, as a result, signatures to classes, functions, and methods regularly include spaces around the equal signs). I realize that this will seem alien to many coders, but it is far easier on my eyes.
  2. I use some so-called "power features", primarily dunder methods, to make my interfaces easier to access and use. This is disfavored in the Google Python Style Guide because such code is often more difficult for others to read. To address that concern, I try to document and comment as to what the code is doing whenever I used any of the "power features" of Python.

Because of the first exception, the project does not use a code formatter (such as ruff format), which would remove those spaces.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: Short solutions to common configuration tasks. Each one assumes import bobbie.

docs.title: Layer local settings over defaults
docs.text:
Keep shared defaults in one file and let each user or machine override some of them in a second file that is not committed:

import pathlib

settings = bobbie.Settings.create('defaults.toml')
local = pathlib.Path('local.toml')
if local.exists():
    settings += bobbie.Settings.create(local)

Because += merges the options within each section, local.toml only needs the options that it changes.

docs.title: Choose settings for an environment
docs.text:
Combine base settings with a file for the current environment, chosen with an environment variable:

import os

environment = os.environ.get('APP_ENV', 'development')
settings = (
    bobbie.Settings.create('settings.toml')
    + bobbie.Settings.create(f'settings.{environment}.toml'))

docs.title: Override settings with environment variables
docs.text:
bobbie does not read environment variables itself, but you can add them as another layer. Here, MYAPP__GENERAL__SEED=7 sets settings['general']['seed']:

import os

overrides: dict[str, dict[str, str]] = {}
for key, value in os.environ.items():
    if key.startswith('MYAPP__'):
        _, section, option = key.lower().split('__', 2)
        overrides.setdefault(section, {})[option] = value
settings += overrides

Environment variables are always strings, so convert the values that need another type.

docs.title: Load a settings file that ships with a package
docs.text:
Use importlib.resources to find a file inside an installed package, even when the package is not a normal folder:

from importlib import resources

source = resources.files('my_package') / 'settings.toml'
with resources.as_file(source) as path:
    settings = bobbie.Settings.create(path)

docs.title: Share one Settings across a project
docs.text:
Load the settings once in a module and import that module wherever the settings are needed:

# my_package/configuration.py
import bobbie

settings = bobbie.Settings.create('settings.toml')

# my_package/analysis.py
from my_package.configuration import settings

seed = settings['general']['seed']

docs.title: Configure a dataclass
docs.text:
To build a dataclass from a section, unpack the section as keyword arguments. This also checks that every option matches a field:

import dataclasses


@dataclasses.dataclass
class FileOptions:
    source_format: str = 'csv'
    file_encoding: str = 'utf-8'


file_options = FileOptions(**settings['files'])

To set attributes on an existing object instead, use inject:

file_options = settings.inject(FileOptions(), sections = 'files')

docs.title: Keep a value as a string
docs.text:
Type inference turns ini and json strings that look like numbers into numbers, so a ZIP code such as 02134 becomes 2134. Store values like this in a toml or yaml file (which keep strings as strings), or turn off inference for the file type before loading:

from bobbie import options

options._INFER_TYPES['ini'] = False
settings = bobbie.Settings.create('addresses.ini')
settings['address']['zip']  # '02134'

Inside a list or dict string, you can also quote an item to keep it a string, as in zips = ['02134', '10001'].

docs.title: Use exact decimals
docs.text:
Load toml or json floats as decimal.Decimal to avoid rounding errors:

import decimal

settings = bobbie.Settings.create('rates.toml', parse_float = decimal.Decimal)

docs.title: Reuse values in an ini file
docs.text:
Turn on configparser interpolation to refer to other options. Options in the DEFAULT section are available in every section:

[DEFAULT]
root = /data

[paths]
raw = %(root)s/raw
processed = %(root)s/processed

import configparser

settings = bobbie.Settings.create(
    'paths.ini', interpolation = configparser.BasicInterpolation())
settings['paths']['raw']  # '/data/raw'

docs.title: Save settings
docs.text:
Use to_file (or the to_ method for the file type) to save settings, such as after changing them in code:

settings['general']['seed'] = 7
settings.to_file('settings.json')

docs.title: Convert a settings file to another format
docs.text:
Load the file and export it with the extension of the new format:

bobbie.Settings.create('settings.ini').to_file('settings.toml')

Values that bobbie infers from an ini or json file keep their inferred types in the new file. For example, seed = 43 in the ini file becomes the toml integer 43, not the string "43".

docs.title: Write a starter settings file
docs.text:
Build the defaults in code and export them, so that users have a file to edit:

defaults = bobbie.Settings({
    'general': {'verbose': False, 'seed': 43},
    'files': {'source_format': 'csv', 'file_encoding': 'utf-8'}})
defaults.to_file('settings.yaml')

docs.title: Pass only some sections to a component
docs.text:
Give a component its own copy of the sections it needs, so that it cannot change the rest of the settings:

model_settings = settings.subset(include = ['model', 'training'])

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: This tutorial walks through the everyday use of bobbie: installing it, loading settings, reading and changing them, and passing them to the rest of a project.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install bobbie with pip:

pip install bobbie

bobbie reads ini, json, toml, and Python module files with the Python standard library. Reading or writing yaml files also requires PyYAML, which you can install with the yaml extra:

pip install "bobbie[yaml]"

The standard library cannot write toml files, so exporting settings to a toml file requires tomli-w, which you can install with the toml extra:

pip install "bobbie[toml]"

docs.title: The Settings class
docs.text:
Everything in bobbie goes through one class, Settings. A Settings instance stores its data in a dict named contents and behaves like a dict, so you can use [], in, len, iteration, keys, values, and items just as you would with a dict.

Project settings are usually organized into sections, each of which is a dict of options:

import bobbie

settings = bobbie.Settings({
    'general': {
        'verbose': False,
        'seed': 43},
    'files': {
        'source_format': 'csv',
        'file_encoding': 'windows-1252'}})

settings['general']['seed']  # 43
'files' in settings  # True
list(settings)  # ['general', 'files']

Several methods (add, update, inject, and the + operator) expect this sectioned layout. See Changing settings below.

docs.title: Creating Settings
docs.text:
There are four ways to create a Settings instance. They all produce the same result.

import bobbie

# 1. Let `create` pick the right constructor for the source.
settings = bobbie.Settings.create('settings.toml')
# 2. Use the constructor for the general kind of source.
settings = bobbie.Settings.from_file('settings.toml')
# 3. Use the constructor for the specific file type.
settings = bobbie.Settings.from_toml('settings.toml')
# 4. Pass a `dict` directly to `Settings`.
settings = bobbie.Settings({'general': {'seed': 43}})

create accepts a str path, a pathlib.Path, or any dict-like object (MutableMapping). Anything else raises a TypeError.

docs.title: Supported files
docs.text:
from_file (and create, when it is given a path) chooses a loader from the file extension:

Extension Loader Parsed with .ini from_ini configparser.ConfigParser .json from_json json.load .py from_module importlib .toml from_toml tomllib.load .yaml, .yml from_yaml yaml.safe_load

A path that does not exist raises a FileNotFoundError, and an unsupported extension raises a TypeError.

Here are the same settings in each format.

tomlyamlinijsonpy 
[general]
verbose = false
seed = 43

[files]
source_format = "csv"
file_encoding = "windows-1252"

[tasks]
things_to_do = ["stop", "drop", "roll"]

general:
    verbose: false
    seed: 43

files:
    source_format: csv
    file_encoding: windows-1252

tasks:
    things_to_do:
        - stop
        - drop
        - roll

[general]
verbose = false
seed = 43

[files]
source_format = csv
file_encoding = windows-1252

[tasks]
things_to_do = stop, drop, roll

{
    "general": {
        "verbose": false,
        "seed": 43
    },
    "files": {
        "source_format": "csv",
        "file_encoding": "windows-1252"
    },
    "tasks": {
        "things_to_do": ["stop", "drop", "roll"]
    }
}

settings = {
    'general': {
        'verbose': False,
        'seed': 43},
    'files': {
        'source_format': 'csv',
        'file_encoding': 'windows-1252'},
    'tasks': {
        'things_to_do': ['stop', 'drop', 'roll']}}

Each of these files loads as the same Settings:

settings = bobbie.Settings.create('settings.ini')
settings['general']['verbose']  # False
settings['tasks']['things_to_do']  # ['stop', 'drop', 'roll']

Python modules

A Python settings file must define a module-level variable named settings that holds the dict of settings. The module is run when it is loaded, so only load modules that you trust. See the Advanced User Guide to use a different variable name.

docs.title: Type inference
docs.text:
ini files store every value as a string, and json files often do, too. So, bobbie converts the values that it loads from those formats to the matching Python types:

Stored string Loaded value '42' 42 '2.5' 2.5 'true', 'yes' (any case) True 'false', 'no' (any case) False '[x, y, z]' ['x', 'y', 'z'] 'x, y, z' ['x', 'y', 'z'] '{a: 1, b: [x, y]}' {'a': 1, 'b': ['x', 'y']} 'csv' 'csv' (unchanged)

Values in toml, yaml, and Python module files are left as they are, because those formats already store their own types. The Advanced User Guide covers the exact rules and how to turn inference on or off for each format.

docs.title: Reading settings
docs.text:
Use [] to read a section or a value:

settings['files']  # {'source_format': 'csv', 'file_encoding': ...}
settings['files']['source_format']  # 'csv'

get returns a fallback for a missing key:

settings.get('database', {})  # {}

get differs from dict.get

If there is no fallback, get raises a KeyError for a missing key instead of returning None. Pass a default or set a default factory if you want missing keys to return something.

keys, values, and items return the same views as a dict:

for section, options in settings.items():
    print(section, options)

To get a plain dict back, use contents (or copy it):

import copy

plain = copy.deepcopy(settings.contents)

docs.title: Changing settings
docs.text:
Assign to a key to add or replace a whole section:

settings['database'] = {'host': 'localhost', 'port': 5432}

add merges options into a section. If the section exists, its options are updated. If it does not, it is created:

settings.add('general', {'seed': 7, 'workers': 4})
settings['general']  # {'verbose': False, 'seed': 7, 'workers': 4}

update calls add for each section in a dict, and += does the same:

settings.update({'general': {'verbose': True}, 'cache': {'size': 100}})
settings += {'cache': {'size': 200}}

+ returns a new Settings that combines both and leaves the original unchanged:

debug_settings = settings + {'general': {'verbose': True}}

Merging is one level deep

add, update, +, and += merge the options within each section. An option whose value is itself a dict is replaced, not merged. Also, adding to an existing key whose value is not a dict (such as settings.add('seed', {...}) when settings['seed'] is 43) raises an AttributeError.

To remove a section, use delete or del:

settings.delete('cache')
del settings['database']

Deleting a missing key does nothing by default. Pass return_error = True to delete to raise a KeyError instead:

settings.delete('cache', return_error = True)  # KeyError

docs.title: Choosing some sections
docs.text:
subset returns a new Settings with only some of the sections. Pass the keys to keep to include, the keys to drop to exclude, or both (include is applied first):

files_only = settings.subset(include = 'files')
no_tasks = settings.subset(exclude = ['tasks'])

The values in the subset are deep copies, so changing them does not change the original. Pass returns = 'simple' to get a plain dict instead of a Settings.

docs.title: Injecting settings into objects
docs.text:
inject copies the options in one or more sections onto an object as attributes. This is a quick way to configure a class instance:

class Loader:
    source_format = None
    file_encoding = 'utf-8'

loader = settings.inject(Loader(), sections = 'files')
loader.source_format  # 'csv'
loader.file_encoding  # 'windows-1252'

Leave out sections to inject every section. Sections that are not in the settings are skipped.

By default, inject overwrites existing attributes. Pass overwrite = False to keep them:

loader = settings.inject(Loader(), sections = 'files', overwrite = False)
loader.source_format  # 'csv' (the existing value, None, was empty)
loader.file_encoding  # 'utf-8'

Note

With overwrite = False, an attribute is only kept if its value is truthy. Attributes that are None, False, 0, or empty are still replaced.

docs.title: Exporting settings to a file
docs.text:
The to_ methods create a settings file from a Settings instance. There is one for each file type (to_ini, to_json, to_module, to_toml, and to_yaml), and to_file picks the right one from the file extension, just as from_file does when loading:

settings = bobbie.Settings.create('settings.yaml')
settings['general']['seed'] = 7

settings.to_file('settings.toml')  # the same as settings.to_toml(...)
settings.to_file('settings.ini')
settings.to_file('settings.py')

An existing file is overwritten. An exported file loads back into the same settings:

bobbie.Settings.create('settings.ini')['general']['seed']  # 7

ini files store every value as a string, so to_ini writes lists and dicts in the form that type inference reads back (such as [stop, drop, roll]). Because ini files only hold values inside sections, every top-level value must be a section (a dict), or to_ini raises a TypeError.

docs.title: Settings(contents=dict(), default_factory=None, name=None) dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Sourcerer, Dictionary

Loads and stores configuration settings.

This class has an interface of an ordinary dict. It also adds class and instance methods that are helpful for project settings, including loading directly from numerous file types, easy injection of settings data as attributes into objects, and smart automatic type conversion from files when appropriate (depending on whether the file type supports typing).

Currently, supported file extensions are:

  • ini, json, py, toml, yaml, and yml.

Settings can also be exported to any of those file types with to_file or the method for the file type (such as to_toml).

The best way to create a Settings instance is to call Settings.create and pass as the first argument either: 1) a pathlib or str path to a compatible file (including a Python module); or 2) a dict or dict-like object.

Any other arguments that you want passed to Settings (such as name) should be passed to the parameters argument. Any additional kwargs that you pass will be relayed to the constructor used by bobbie. For example, bobbie uses the builtin tomllib library to parse toml files. If you want to change the float parser to decimal.Decimal when loading settings from a ".toml" file and name your Settings instance "Project Settings", you should do this:

Settings.create(
    'configuration.toml',
    parameters = {'name': 'Project Settings'},
    parse_float = decimal.Decimal)

You may also instance Settings directly, like a normal class. However, doing so precludes the ability to relay additional keyword arguments to the constructor used by bobbie (parse_float in the above example).

def add(  # type: ignore[override]
        self,
        key: Hashable,
        value: GenericDict) -> None:
    """Adds `key` and `value` to `contents`.

    If `key` is already a key in `contents`, the contents associated with
    that key are updated. If `key` doesn't exist, a new key/value pair is
    added to `contents`.

    Args:
        key: name of key to store `value`.
        value: values to be stored.

    Raises:
        TypeError: if `key` isn't hashable.

    """
    try:
        self[key].update(value)
    except KeyError:
        try:
            self[key] = value
        except TypeError as error:
            message = 'The key must be hashable'
            raise TypeError(message) from error
    return

def delete(
        self,
        key: Hashable,
        return_error: bool | None = None) -> None:
    """Deletes `key` in `contents`.

    Args:
        key: key in `contents` to delete the key/value pair.
        return_error: returns error if `key` is missing. Defaults to None
            (which will result in the global setting stored in
            `options._ALWAYS_RETURN_ERROR` being used).

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `key` is not in `contents` and `return_error` is
            True.
        TypeError: if `key` isn't hashable.

    """
    if return_error is None:
        return_error = options._ALWAYS_RETURN_ERROR
    try:
        del self.contents[key]
    except KeyError as error:
        if return_error:
            message = f'{key} is not found in the settings'
            raise KeyError(message) from error
    except TypeError as error:
        message = 'The key must be hashable'
        raise TypeError(message) from error
    return

@create.register(str | pathlib.Path)
@classmethod
def from_file(
        cls,
        source: str | pathlib.Path,
        /,
        parameters: MutableMapping[str, Any] | None = None,
        **kwargs: Any) -> Settings:
    """Creates a `Settings` instance from a file path.

    Args:
        source: path to file with data to store in a `Settings` instance.
        parameters: additional parameters and arguments to pass to the
            created `Settings` instance. Defaults to None.
        **kwargs: additional parameters and arguments to pass to the
            constructor used by `bobbie` (such as `encoding`).

    Returns:
        A `Settings` instance derived from `source`.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: if the `source` path does not correspond to a
            file.
        TypeError: if no constructor method is found for the passed file
            type or `parameters` has an argument that `Settings` does not
            accept.

    """
    path = utilities._pathlibify(source)
    loader = cls._get_loader(path)
    settings: Settings = loader(path, **kwargs)
    if parameters:
        # Rebuilds the instance so that `parameters` are passed to the
        # constructor, as they are by `from_dict`.
        settings = dataclasses.replace(settings, **parameters)
    return settings

def from_ini(cls, source: pathlib.Path | str, **kwargs: Any) -> Settings:
    """Creates a `Settings` instance from a file path to an `ini` file.

    Comments after values (a "#" with whitespace before and after it, to
    the end of its line) are removed unless `options._INLINE_COMMENTS` is
    `False`.

    Args:
        source: path to file with data to store in a `Settings` instance.
        **kwargs: additional parameters and arguments to pass to the
            `configparser.ConfigParser` constructor (such as
            `interpolation`), except for `encoding`, which is the file
            encoding (defaults to 'utf-8').

    Returns:
        A `Settings` instance derived from `source`.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: if the `source` path does not correspond to a
            file.

    """
    path = utilities._pathlibify(source)
    import configparser

    if not path.is_file():
        message = f'settings file {path} not found'
        raise FileNotFoundError(message)
    encoding = kwargs.pop('encoding', 'utf-8')
    # Interpolation is turned off by default so that values such as '%.4f'
    # are not treated as `configparser` interpolation syntax.
    kwargs.setdefault('interpolation', None)
    parser = configparser.ConfigParser(**kwargs)
    parser.optionxform = lambda option: option  # type: ignore
    parser.read(path, encoding = encoding)
    # Uses `dict` types so that the implicit "DEFAULT" section is not
    # included as a section of its own (its values are already part of
    # every other section).
    contents: GenericDict = {
        name: dict(parser[name]) for name in parser.sections()}
    if options._INLINE_COMMENTS:
        contents = {
            name: {
                key: utilities._strip_inline_comments(value)
                if isinstance(value, str) else value
                for key, value in section.items()}
            for name, section in contents.items()}
    if options._INFER_TYPES['ini']:
        contents = cls._infer_types(contents)
    return cls(contents)

def from_module(
        cls,
        source: pathlib.Path | str,
        **kwargs: Any) -> Settings:
    """Creates a `Settings` instance from a file path to a Python module.

    The settings are read from the module-level variable named in
    `options._MODULE_SETTINGS_ATTRIBUTE` ('settings' by default).

    Args:
        source: path to file with data to store in a `Settings` instance.
        **kwargs: additional parameters and arguments to pass to
            `importlib.util.spec_from_file_location`.

    Returns:
        A `Settings` instance derived from `source`.

    Raises:
        AttributeError: if the module does not have a variable named in
            `options._MODULE_SETTINGS_ATTRIBUTE`.
        FileNotFoundError: if the `source` path does not correspond to a
            file.

    """
    path = utilities._pathlibify(source)
    name = options._MODULE_SETTINGS_ATTRIBUTE
    try:
        specer = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location
        import_path = specer(path.name, path, **kwargs)
        import_module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(
            import_path)  # type: ignore
        import_path.loader.exec_module(import_module)  # type: ignore
    except FileNotFoundError as error:
        message = f'settings file {path} not found'
        raise FileNotFoundError(message) from error
    try:
        contents = getattr(import_module, name)
    except AttributeError as error:
        message = f'settings file {path} has no variable named {name}'
        raise AttributeError(message) from error
    if options._INFER_TYPES['module']:
        contents = cls._infer_types(contents)
    return cls(contents)

def inject(
        self,
        instance: object,
        sections: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
        overwrite: bool | None = None) -> object:
    """Injects appropriate items into `instance` from `contents`.

    Each key/value pair in the chosen sections is added to `instance` as
    an attribute. Sections missing from `contents` are skipped.

    Args:
        instance: class instance to be modified.
        sections: other section(s) in `contents` to add to `instance`.
            Defaults to None (which will result in all sections being
            injected).
        overwrite: whether to overwrite a local attribute in `instance` if
            there are existing values stored in that attribute. Defaults to
            None (which will result in the default value in
            `_OVERWRITE_ATTRIBUTES` will be used).

    Returns:
        Instance with modifications made.

    """
    overwrite = (
        options._OVERWRITE_ATTRIBUTES if overwrite is None else overwrite)
    names = self.keys() if sections is None else sections
    for section in utilities._iterify(names):
        with contextlib.suppress(KeyError):
            for key, value in self.contents[section].items():
                if (
                        not hasattr(instance, key)
                        or not getattr(instance, key)
                        or overwrite):
                    setattr(instance, key, value)
    return instance

def subset(
        self,
        include: Collection[Any] | Any | None = None,
        exclude: Collection[Any] | Any | None = None,
        returns: SubsetReturns | None = None) -> Any:
    """Returns a new instance with a subset of `contents`.

    This method applies `include` before `exclude` if both are passed. If
    `include` is None, all existing items will be added to the new subset
    class instance before `exclude` is applied. The values in the subset
    are deep copies, so changing them does not change this instance.

    Args:
        include: key(s) to include in the new `Dictionary`. Defaults to
            `None`.
        exclude: key(s) to exclude from the new `Dictionary`. Defaults to
            `None`.
        returns: whether to return a new instance of the `Dictionary`
            subclass ("class"), a deep copy of the subclass instance
            ("copy") or the simple native Python type ("simple"). Defaults
            to `None`, which uses the global setting stored in
            `settings._SUBSET_RETURN`.

    Returns:
        `dict`-like object with only keys from `include` and no keys in
            `exclude`, in the form dictated by the `returns` argument.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if `include` and `exclude` are both None.
        KeyError: if a key in `include` is not in `contents`.

    """
    if include is None and exclude is None:
        raise ValueError('include or exclude must not be None')
    returns = self._resolve_returns(returns)
    if include is None:
        keys = list(self.contents)
    else:
        keys = list(utilities._iterify(include))
    if exclude is not None:
        excluded = list(utilities._iterify(exclude))
        keys = [k for k in keys if k not in excluded]
    contents = copy.deepcopy({k: self.contents[k] for k in keys})
    return utilities._return_subset(
        subset = contents, existing = self, returns = returns)

def to_ini(self, path: pathlib.Path | str, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    """Exports `contents` to an `ini` file.

    Every top-level value must be a section (a `dict`-like object) because
    `ini` files do not allow values outside of sections. Values are
    converted to strings that `from_ini` converts back to their datatypes
    (for example, `['x', 'y']` becomes '[x, y]'). Because `ini` files do not
    store types, a str that looks like another type (such as '42') is
    loaded as that type. Unless `options._INLINE_COMMENTS` is `False`, a
    "#" with whitespace before and after it in a value is loaded as the
    start of a comment.

    Args:
        path: path of the file to write. An existing file is overwritten.
        **kwargs: additional parameters and arguments to pass to the
            `configparser.ConfigParser` constructor (such as
            `delimiters`), except for `encoding`, which is the file
            encoding (defaults to 'utf-8').

    Raises:
        TypeError: if a top-level value in `contents` is not a `dict`-like
            object.

    """
    path = utilities._pathlibify(path)
    import configparser

    for key, value in self.contents.items():
        if not isinstance(value, MutableMapping):
            message = f'{key} must be a section (a mapping) in ini files'
            raise TypeError(message)
    encoding = kwargs.pop('encoding', 'utf-8')
    # Interpolation is turned off by default to match `from_ini`, so that
    # values such as '%.4f' are written as they are.
    kwargs.setdefault('interpolation', None)
    parser = configparser.ConfigParser(**kwargs)
    parser.optionxform = lambda option: option  # type: ignore
    parser.read_dict({
        str(name): {
            str(key): utilities._stringify(value)
            for key, value in section.items()}
        for name, section in self.contents.items()})
    with open(path, 'w', encoding = encoding) as settings_file:
        parser.write(settings_file)
    return
